In 1945, Kellogg's inserted a [prize](/wiki/Cereal_box_prize "Cereal box prize") in the form of [pin-back buttons](/wiki/Pin-back_button "Pin-back button") into each box of Pep cereal. Pep pins have included [U.S. Army](/wiki/U.S._Army "U.S. Army") squadrons as well as characters from newspaper comics and were available through 1947. There were five series of comic characters and 18 different buttons in each set, with a total of 90 in the collection.[[93]](#cite_note-promomagazine.com-93) Other manufacturers of major brands of cereal, including [General Mills](/wiki/General_Mills "General Mills"), [Malt-O-Meal](/wiki/Malt-O-Meal_Company "Malt-O-Meal Company"), [Nestlé](/wiki/Nestl%C3%A9 "Nestlé"), [Post Foods](/wiki/Post_Foods "Post Foods"), and [Quaker Oats](/wiki/Quaker_Oats_Company "Quaker Oats Company"), followed suit and inserted prizes into boxes of cereal to promote sales and brand loyalty.

The [Wright Company](/wiki/Wright_Company "Wright Company") was incorporated on November 22, 1909. In mid-1910, the Wrights changed the design of the *Wright Flyer*, moving the horizontal elevator from the front to the back and adding wheels although keeping the skids as part of the undercarriage unit. It had become apparent by then that a rear elevator would make an airplane easier to control, especially as higher speeds grew more common. The new version was designated the "Model B", although the original canard design was never referred to as the "Model A" by the Wrights. However, the U.S. Army Signal Corps which bought the airplane did call it "Wright type A".[[155]](#cite_note-163)

There were not many customers for airplanes, so in early 1910 the Wrights hired and trained the [Wright Exhibition Team](/wiki/Wright_Exhibition_Team "Wright Exhibition Team") of salaried pilots to show off their machines and win prize money for the company – despite Wilbur's disdain for what he called "the [mountebank](/wiki/Charlatan "Charlatan") business". The [Squaxin](/wiki/Squaxin "Squaxin") and other [Coast Salish](/wiki/Coast_Salish "Coast Salish") peoples inhabited the southern Puget Sound region prior to the arrival of European and American settlers in the 19th century. The [Treaty of Medicine Creek](/wiki/Treaty_of_Medicine_Creek "Treaty of Medicine Creek") was signed in 1854 and followed by the Treaty of Olympia in 1856; these two treaties forced the Squaxin to relocate to an [Indian reservation](/wiki/Indian_reservation "Indian reservation"). Olympia was declared the capital of the [Washington Territory](/wiki/Washington_Territory "Washington Territory") in 1853 and incorporated as a town on January 28, 1859. It became a city in 1882.

Aside from its role in the state government, Olympia is also recognized as a countercultural hub in the Pacific Northwest. The city's [music scene](/wiki/Music_of_Olympia,_Washington "Music of Olympia, Washington") gained prominence in the 1990s for its role in the emergence of [punk rock](/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") movements such as [riot grrrl](/wiki/Riot_grrrl "Riot grrrl") and [grunge](/wiki/Grunge "Grunge"). The Olympia area is also home to [The Evergreen State College](/wiki/The_Evergreen_State_College "The Evergreen State College"), a public liberal arts institution known for its non-traditional curriculum. [Intercity Transit](/wiki/Intercity_Transit "Intercity Transit") provides fare-free bus service throughout the Olympia area, which has high per-capita use of public transportation relative to other cities of its size.

Al Carder notes that in 1888 a cash reward of 100 pounds was offered there for the discovery of any tree measuring more than 400 feet (120 m).[[48]](#cite_note-Carder-48) The fact that such a considerable reward was never claimed is taken as evidence that such large trees did not exist. Carder's historical research, however, revealed that the reward was offered under conditions that made it highly unlikely to be collected. First, it was made in the depths of winter and applied only for a very short time. Next, the tree had to be measured by an accredited surveyor. Since loggers had already taken the largest trees from the most accessible Victorian forests, finding very tall trees then would have demanded an arduous trek into remote wilderness and at considerable altitude. In turn, that meant that searchers also needed the services of experienced bushmen to be able to guide them and conduct an effective search.
